edges.label: COMPARISON: publish the raw record and disclaim competence, versus publish the adjudicated case file
edges.note: COMPARISON EDGE — no contact between the Arquivo Nacional and GEIPAN is claimed. Two different theories of state openness. GEIPAN is the investigating office itself publishing a searchable, four-tier-classified case database out of CNES; the Brazilian arrangement is the opposite shape — the military transfers scanned raw records into a civil archive and then says it has no specialists qualified to investigate or to offer an opinion. Brazil gives the citizen the primary document and no adjudication; France gives the citizen the adjudication. The board should not treat these as the same category of openness. Tier 2 because the comparison is analytic; the underlying facts on each side are separately sourced on the two nodes.

b.label: Sky Canada Project - Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada

edges.label: COMPARISON: Canada surveyed the world's UAP-reporting models and did not mention Brazil once
edges.note: COMPARISON EDGE, and a second sourced negative. The Sky Canada Project report examined 'the management of UAP reporting in several countries' and concluded that 'the processes in place in a few countries, notably the United States, France and Chile, provide interesting examples of coordinated, transparent, and scientifically driven approaches'. Its recommendation 13 tells the future Canadian lead organisation to 'establish partnerships with international entities dedicated to UAPs, such as AARO and NASA (U.S.A.), GEIPAN (France), and SEFAA (Chile).' The word 'Brazil' does not occur in the report. The state that actually put its military UAP files in a public archive is absent from the survey of states that handle UAP reporting well — which is a finding about the survey as much as about Brazil.
